Do developers trust AI? Adoption, attitudes and pay in the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey

A complex data analysis in R

29 September 2026

1 Introduction

AI coding assistants moved from novelty to default tooling in about three years. This report uses the Stack Overflow Annual Developer Survey 2025 (44,682 professional developers after cleaning, 175 countries) to ask who actually adopts them, who trusts them, and whether any of it shows up in pay.

1.1 Research questions

# Question Method
RQ1 Does AI tool adoption depend on developer role and experience? Chi-square, logistic regression
RQ2 Do AI users earn more than non-users? Welch t-test, Wilcoxon, linear regression
RQ3 Does trust in AI accuracy change with experience? Chi-square, test for trend
RQ4 Can AI adoption be predicted from professional attributes? Logistic regression vs random forest
RQ5 Are there distinct developer “personas” in AI attitudes? PCA, k-means

1.2 Key findings

  1. Adoption is near-universal but shallow in trust. 79.4% use AI tools and 48.1% use them daily, yet only 32.4% say they trust the accuracy of what those tools produce.
  2. Both adoption and trust fall as experience rises. Adoption drops from 88.5% among developers with 0-2 years of experience to 72.7% among those with 20+ years (chi-square test for trend, p < 0.001).
  3. AI users earn slightly less, not more. Median $76,097 versus $81,685 (Cohen’s d = -0.16). The gap is a small effect and is explained by experience and region rather than by AI use itself.
  4. Pay is mostly explained by geography, experience and education. The linear model reaches R² = 0.443; AI use contributes almost nothing once those are in the model.
  5. Adoption is hard to predict from professional attributes. The best model reaches AUC 0.6632 (5-fold CV) — better than chance, far from decisive.
  6. The complaint is precision, not capability. 67% name “AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite” as a frustration, and 46% say debugging AI-generated code is more time-consuming than writing it themselves.
  7. Developers split into two clear camps. k-means finds 2 clusters: an AI-embracing group (54.5% of respondents, 87% daily users) and a sceptical group (45.5%, 24% daily users). The sceptics have a higher median salary ($83,668 versus $73,686) — salary was never used to build the clusters.

1.3 Data and licence

Stack Overflow Annual Developer Survey 2025, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://survey.stackoverflow.co/. The raw file holds 172 columns; the cleaning script keeps 38 after feature engineering and restricts the sample to people who write code professionally.

2 Data preparation

The raw export needs real work before it can be analysed:

  • Types. YearsCode is text because of the answers “Less than 1 year” and “More than 50 years”; Age is a bucket, converted to a midpoint for modelling while the ordered factor is kept for plots.
  • Collapsing. Education (8 levels), organisation size (9), and country (180+) are collapsed to 4, 3 and 6 categories. Rare roles and industries are lumped with fct_lump_min(). Without this, most tests would be driven by categories with a handful of respondents.
  • Salary. ConvertedCompYearly contains values from $1 to tens of millions. Values below $1,000 or above the 99th percentile are flagged (comp_outlier) rather than deleted, and the models use log(salary) because the distribution is log-normal.
  • Multi-select columns. LanguageHaveWorkedWith and AIModelsHaveWorkedWith hold semicolon-separated lists; they are split with separate_rows() for counting and turned into breadth counts (n_languages, n_ai_models) for modelling.
  • Likert scales. Sentiment and trust become ordered factors and numeric scores, so they can be both plotted as categories and correlated.
fig("01_missingness")
Missing values by variable

Missingness is concentrated in the optional free-text and compensation fields, which is why every model states the row count it actually fits on.

3.4 What developers think survives AI

The survey ends with an open question: “Looking ahead 3-5 years, what skills do you believe will remain valuable for developers even as AI tools become more capable?” A simple word count over the 17,456 free-text answers shows what people name.

fig("11_ai_open_words")
Skills expected to remain valuable

The answers cluster on judgement rather than syntax: understanding, problem solving, architecture, design and debugging. That matches the trust results — developers delegate typing, not deciding.

4 Statistical inference

Every test reports an assumption check, an effect size and a confidence interval where one exists. Because five families of hypotheses are tested, p-values are adjusted with the Holm method.

A note on interpretation: with tens of thousands of respondents, almost anything reaches statistical significance. The effect sizes matter more than the p-values, which is why Cramer’s V, Cohen’s d and eta-squared are reported alongside every test.

Majority-class baseline NA 0.8116 NA NA NA 0.5000 NA NA NA NA NA

Four in five respondents use AI tools, so a model that predicts “user” for everyone already scores 81.2% accuracy while being useless. The decision threshold is therefore tuned on the training set (Youden’s J) rather than left at 0.5, which trades raw accuracy for a model that actually separates the two groups — and makes AUC, not accuracy, the metric worth reading in that table.

fig("15_roc_curves")
ROC curves
fig("16_rf_importance")
Random forest importance

The two models land close together, which is itself the finding: the relationship between professional attributes and AI adoption is mostly additive, so the random forest’s extra flexibility buys little. Both beat the majority-class baseline, but neither is a strong classifier — adoption is driven by things the survey does not measure (team policy, employer tooling, personal taste).

The validation table is the point of this section: salary, remote work and organisation size were deliberately excluded from the clustering features, so differences across clusters on those variables are evidence that the personas capture something real rather than an artefact of the algorithm.

7 Limitations

  • Self-selected sample. Respondents are Stack Overflow visitors who chose to answer; they over-represent North America and Europe, so nothing here generalises to the whole developer population.
  • Cross-sectional. Every association is correlational. Higher earners using AI more does not mean AI raised anyone’s salary; both are downstream of employer, seniority and country.
  • Converted compensation. ConvertedCompYearly depends on exchange rates and self-reported figures, and the currency conversion date is not exposed.
  • Collapsed categories. Grouping 180 countries into 6 regions and 8 education levels into 4 loses real variation. It trades precision for models that fit and tests that have adequate cell counts.
  • Large n. Statistical significance is nearly guaranteed at this sample size; effect sizes are the honest summary.

8 Reproducing this report

Rscript scripts/00_setup.R     # install packages, download data (~141 MB)
Rscript scripts/run_all.R      # clean, analyse, model, render this report

All randomness is seeded (SEED = 42 in R/setup.R), so reruns reproduce the same splits, folds and clusters.
